methodological_rigor.justification: The cross-sectional survey has a reasonably sized analytic sample (n = 518 with complete data from 736 starters) recruited through a health system EDW with defined eligibility criteria, and outcomes are operationalized with standard measures (Godin LTEQ). However, the analysis is restricted to separate univariate logistic regressions for each demographic/health variable against each of three outcomes, with no multivariable adjustment, no correction for multiple testing across many bivariate comparisons (14+ predictors x 3 outcomes), and no sensitivity analyses. Missing data handling (218 excluded from 736 completers) is not described, risking selection bias. No pre-registration.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a single-center cross-sectional survey of cancer survivors from one health system, which aligns with Oxford LoE 4 (case series / low-quality cross-sectional study). The topic is clinically relevant to survivorship care and digital health integration, and findings inform practical strategies (e.g., EHR integration, loan programs, equity considerations). However, the absence of any intervention or outcome beyond self-reported ownership limits direct clinical utility, and the predominantly White, highly educated sample reduces generalizability as the authors acknowledge.

reporting_quality.justification: As a cross-sectional observational study, STROBE is the applicable standard. Most core items are addressed: study setting, eligibility, measures, variables, and statistical methods. Participant flow is reported narratively (759 consented, 736 completed, 518 complete). Key gaps: no STROBE checklist mentioned, no missing data handling described, no flow diagram, and many CIs straddle 1 yet significance statements are generous. Data availability is not addressed; no statement on code or repository sharing is provided.

novelty_literature.justification: The study replicates prior HINTS-based analyses (Zhou, Gitonga) with a single-health-system sample and finds similar socioeconomic correlates of mHealth adoption. Authors explicitly compare their findings to these prior studies and explain higher ownership (56% vs 29%, 41%) as a secular trend. The disaggregation of specific apps and devices (Apple Watch, Fitbit, MyFitnessPal, Peloton) is a useful but minor addition. The willingness-to-share outcome yields mostly null results. Overall the contribution is incremental confirmation.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with a logical structure (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) and readable prose. The Discussion is thorough and well-referenced, though some paragraphs (particularly on EHR integration strategies) are long and would benefit from subheadings. Tables are appropriately referenced. There is a minor inconsistency (abstract reports 32.4% app use vs 32.43% in Results; 52.9% vs 52.90% tracker ownership; sample sometimes described as 2023 collection, elsewhere 2024). Overall the paper communicates effectively.

key_strengths: Adequately sized survey (n = 518) from a single large health system EDW with clear eligibility criteria and standard measures (Godin LTEQ, PA guidelines)
Disaggregated reporting of specific apps (MyFitnessPal, Peloton, Strava) and devices (Apple Watch, Fitbit), which adds granularity beyond prior HINTS-based studies
Practical discussion of EHR integration, equity considerations, and strategies for engaging underserved survivors
Transparent acknowledgement of homogeneous sample and self-report limitations
key_concerns: Only univariate logistic regressions performed; no multivariable adjustment for confounding among correlated demographics
No correction for multiple testing across 14+ predictors x 3 outcomes; risk of inflated Type I error
218 participants excluded due to incomplete data with no missing-data handling rationale
Largely incremental findings that replicate prior HINTS-based work; novelty limited
Inconsistent data-collection year reporting (2023 in Methods vs 2024 in Discussion)
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competently written but methodologically modest survey paper with univariate-only analyses and incremental findings. It is best suited to a Tier 4 survivorship or digital-health journal with minor revisions to address multiple-testing, missing data, and inconsistencies.
